title: A reusable editorial rule did not preserve the intended hierarchy
description: In this comparison, adding a generic instruction to preserve Synthesis’s editorial intent did not keep the company-level message primary. All three candidate Narrative runs made orchestration central and introduced unsupported framing; all three Compose runs also failed the hierarchy and factual-restraint gates. The candidate scored lower on average in both stages, so it was not promoted and the production prompt was restored. This is evidence about these runs, not proof that the rule will fail in every setting.
audience: People designing or evaluating multi-stage AI editorial workflows.
rationale: The experiment tests a specific prompt intervention against explicit editorial criteria and records a clear decision. It also shows why a prompt change should be judged by whether it preserves the intended message, not just whether the output reads smoothly.
evidence: Fact: The candidate changed only the Narrative user prompt; candidate Narrative and Compose mean scores were lower than baseline, and every candidate run failed the orchestration-hierarchy and factual-restraint gates. The decision was not to promote, and the production prompt was restored byte-for-byte. Inference: The generic rule was insufficient to protect the intended hierarchy in this test. Unknown: Three runs per condition do not establish statistical significance or general performance across settings.

title: The source itself contains a tension over orchestration’s importance
description: The baseline Synthesis pairs Nuëyon’s identity and Compose in its top-level emphasis, but later calls orchestration “central to the product direction.” The report suggests this internal tension may have reinforced the technical framing, while noting that the experiment did not change Synthesis. That is a plausible diagnostic, not an established cause of the candidate outputs.
audience: People reviewing how editorial emphasis moves between stages of an AI-assisted content workflow.
rationale: It identifies a source-level ambiguity that matters to the experiment’s intended hierarchy, while keeping a possible explanation separate from the measured result.
evidence: Fact: The report describes both the top-level emphasis and the later orchestration statement in baseline Synthesis, and says Synthesis was outside the experiment’s scope. The report says the tension may have reinforced the technical angle. Unknown: The experiment did not test whether revising Synthesis would change Narrative or Compose outputs.

title: Readable, coherent output can still lose source fidelity
description: Candidate prose remained generally readable and coherent, yet its source-fidelity ratings were consistently lower and its intended company-level message was displaced by technical exposition. In this evaluation, surface quality and editorial fidelity did not move together.
audience: Teams assessing generated editorial content for both prose quality and faithfulness to source priorities.
rationale: The results distinguish fluent writing from successful preservation of message hierarchy, a distinction the experiment’s separate scoring categories make visible.
evidence: Fact: Both conditions were generally rated 4/5 for readability and coherence; candidate Narrative and Compose outputs were consistently rated 2/5 for source fidelity, compared with baseline ranges of 2–3/5. The report describes orchestration becoming central and unsupported additions appearing in candidate outputs. Inference: Readability and coherence scores alone would not capture the editorial drift observed here. Unknown: The subjective ratings do not establish how these qualities relate in other experiments.
